title: Discourse on the Logic of Language
description: A poem by M. NourbeSe Philip in She Tries Her Tongue, Her Silence Softly Breaks (1989): a page-spanning collage in which a stuttering verse on English as 'my mother tongue' and 'a foreign anguish' is set beside a story of a mother licking her newborn daughter, two edicts on the treatment of slaves' languages, and textbook passages on the brain.
plot_or_argument: The central verse begins 'English / is my mother tongue', then breaks down: a mother tongue is not a foreign lan lan lang, language, l/anguish, anguish, a foreign anguish. English is her father tongue, and she has no mother tongue, only a 'dumb-tongued', 'dub-tongued' speech, and she asks what she is to do. Beside it, in capitals, a narrative tells of a mother who licks her newborn daughter clean and blows her own words, her mother's words, into the child's mouth. Two edicts in italics, in the cool voice of administration, advise slave owners to mix their slaves of different language groups so that they cannot plot rebellion, and order that any slave caught speaking his native language have his tongue removed. Passages in the style of a physiology textbook describe the brain's speech centres and nineteenth-century theories of racial difference, and the poem ends with a multiple-choice test on the tongue.
narrative_structure: Several texts on the page at once, verse in the centre, the mother's story in a margin, edicts and textbook passages elsewhere, so that the page must be read in more than one direction.
literary_form: Poem (multi-voiced text of verse, prose and edicts)
meter_and_prosody: Stammering repetition and wordplay (language, languish, anguish), capitals, italics and documentary registers set against each other; collage and fragmentation.
historical_context: She Tries Her Tongue, Her Silence Softly Breaks won the Casa de las Américas Prize in manuscript and was published in 1989; it belongs to the Caribbean debates on nation language and to the feminist writing of black women in Canada.
literary_significance: Philip's most anthologised poem and a central text of Caribbean and Canadian experimental writing on language, much taught and studied.
bibliographical_notes: Published in She Tries Her Tongue, Her Silence Softly Breaks (Charlottetown: Ragweed Press, 1989). A selection of The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 11th edition, vol. F, beginning on page 743.
thematic_analysis: The violence of colonial and slave history embodied in language: English as the imposed father tongue and the mother tongue that survives in secret transmission between women. The poem exposes the apparent objectivity of the coloniser's discourses, legal and scientific, and makes the reader's difficulty part of its meaning.
summary: The speaker's verse on English as mother tongue and father tongue; a narrative of a mother blowing words into her child's mouth; Edicts I and II on separating slaves by language and cutting out the tongue of any slave who speaks it; scientific accounts of the speech centres of the brain; a multiple-choice question.
critical_context: Critics read it through Brathwaite's nation language, Bhabha's in-betweenness and theories of the violence of language, as deconstructing the apparent objectivity and logic of English; reviewers of the book quoted its 'foreign anguish' as its key pun.
research_notes: The publisher is general knowledge. Wikipedia also lists Discourse on the Logic of Language (1989) as a separate item, presumably a separate printing, which was not checked. Details of the edicts and textbook passages are stated from general knowledge of the text and corroborated by student and review extracts that were not cited.

title: The Prophet's Hair
description: A short story by Salman Rushdie, first published in the London Review of Books on 16 April 1981 and collected, revised, in East, West (1994). In Srinagar, a secular moneylender who comes upon the stolen relic of the Prophet Muhammad's hair becomes a tyrannical zealot, with disastrous results for his family.
plot_or_argument: In a fierce winter in Srinagar, the moneylender's son Atta goes into the city's most dangerous quarter to hire a thief and is beaten nearly to death. The story then explains. Hashim, a rich moneylender who prides himself on his rational, honourable life, found floating in the lake a silver phial holding the famous hair of the Prophet, stolen the previous morning from the shrine at Hazratbal. A collector, he decided to keep it. At once he changed: he ordered his family to read the holy book for hours each day, forbade the cinema, told terrible truths about his marriage and his mistress, insulted his son and accused his daughter Huma of lewdness, and beat her. When Atta tried to return the relic it seemed to come back to the house by itself. Huma hires the thief Sheikh Sin to steal it; but on the night, Hashim, waking, grabs a sword, rushes out, and in the darkness kills his daughter, and then himself; the injured Atta dies, and Hashim's wife goes mad. The relic is restored to the shrine, and the thief's crippled sons, miraculously cured, lose their living as beggars.
narrative_structure: A short story opening in medias res and moving back through flashback to the climactic night and an ironic coda.
meter_and_prosody: Long, rolling sentences full of clauses, wit and Kashmiri detail; magical realism handled with comic deadpan.
historical_context: The story draws on the theft of the relic from the Hazratbal shrine in December 1963 and its recovery about two weeks later; Rushdie wrote it for the London Review of Books in the year of Midnight's Children. After the Satanic Verses affair its subject gained new resonance.
literary_significance: One of Rushdie's most anthologised stories, read as a parable of religious zeal and a forecast of the themes of his later work.
bibliographical_notes: First published in the London Review of Books, vol. 3, no. 7 (16 April 1981); collected in a revised version in East, West (London: Jonathan Cape, 1994). A selection of The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 11th edition, vol. F, beginning on page 1064.
thematic_analysis: Religious fanaticism as a possession that destroys the possessor; the clash of secular rationalism and faith; greed and the urge to collect; the comic and terrible ironies of miracles.
summary: Hashim the moneylender keeps the relic stolen from the Hazratbal shrine; its effect on him and his household; his children's plan to have it stolen back by the master thief Sheikh Sin; the night on which everything goes wrong.
research_notes: The LRB page (seen as a search extract) confirms the date and parts of the plot; the rest of the plot is stated from general knowledge of the text and agrees with study summaries that were not cited. The Hazratbal theft of 1963, the revision for East, West and its publisher are general knowledge.

title: Imaginary Homelands
description: Salman Rushdie's Imaginary Homelands: Essays and Criticism 1981-1991 (London: Granta, in association with Penguin, 1991), a collection of essays and reviews whose title essay calls the migrant the central or defining figure of the twentieth century. Norton prints two bracketed excerpts from it.
plot_or_argument: The title essay, first printed in the London Review of Books on 7 October 1982, begins from Rushdie's attempt to recover the Bombay of his childhood in Midnight's Children and argues that exiles and migrants, looking back, create not actual cities or villages but imaginary homelands, fragmentary and partial, whose broken mirror is a truth of its own. Comparing his novel with other literature of diaspora, he claims that the migrant, whether from one country, language or culture to another or from a traditional village to a modern city, is perhaps the central or defining figure of the twentieth century, and that writers of the Indian diaspora in Britain may claim English and the English tradition as their own. Other essays dispute the category of 'Commonwealth literature', review contemporary novelists, attack the politics of Thatcher's Britain and its racism, and, in the later pieces, respond to the attacks on The Satanic Verses.
narrative_structure: Essays, lectures and reviews of 1981-1991, grouped in sections by subject, with the title essay first.
meter_and_prosody: Witty, combative, conversational prose, mixing memoir, polemic and close reading.
historical_context: Published two years into the fatwa, the book gathered a decade of Rushdie's journalism, lectures and criticism, from the years of Midnight's Children to the Satanic Verses affair.
literary_significance: A key statement of migrant and postcolonial writing in Britain; its title has become a common term for the imagined homelands of diaspora.
bibliographical_notes: Imaginary Homelands: Essays and Criticism 1981-1991 (London: Granta Books, in association with Penguin, 1991). Norton's two excerpts, '[The British Indian Writer and a Dream-England]' and '[English Is an Indian Literary Language]', are selections of The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 11th edition, vol. F, beginning on pages 747 and 750.
thematic_analysis: Migration and memory, the right of the migrant writer to English and to many traditions, the politics of Britain, India and Pakistan, and the freedom of literature.
summary: Essays on India, Pakistan and Britain, on politics (the assassination of Indira Gandhi, the 1983 general election, censorship, the Labour Party, Palestinian identity), on the Satanic Verses affair, and on writers including Naipaul, Greene, Barnes and Ishiguro, with the title essay on memory, migration and Midnight's Children.
research_notes: The essays from which Norton's two excerpts come were not identified; the second is commonly taken from "'Commonwealth Literature' Does Not Exist" (1983), which is general knowledge, not checked. The summary of the title essay beyond Wikipedia's account (the broken mirror, the claim to English), the grouping of the essays and the essays beyond those Wikipedia names are general knowledge.
